Beast of the Apocalypse BY GRAHAM EDWARDS t is common in fantasy literature for the hero - whether noble warrior or meek underling - to discover that fate has set him unexpectedly on the path to greatness. In the Dark Horse Books comic Hellboy: The Wild Hunt, the half-demon Hellboy must vanquish the evil sorceress Nimue by transforming himself into the all-powerful Beast of the Apocalypse and unleashing an army from the underworld. This is the destiny laid out for him by his satanic father, as Hellboy is told: "He created you to set free all those enslaved in Hell." But there is a catch - freeing Hell's minions will also wipe out all life on Earth. Caught on the horns of a devilish dilemma, Hellboy responds in typical fashion: "Screw that!" This quandary is central to the story of Lionsgate's Hellboy, the third feature film featuring the demonic paranormal investigator created by writer/artist Mike Mignola. Adhering closely to the narrative of The Wild Hunt, the film also draws material from the related Hellboy volumes Darkness Calls and The Storm and the Fury, and stars David Harbour as the horned hero. Accompanying Hellboy on his latest adventure are Alice Monaghan (Sasha Lane), an Irish woman whose life is inextricably linked to the fairy 1 / 30 realm, and Ben Daimio (Daniel Dae Kim), one of Hellboy's fellow operatives at the Bureau

HELLBOY for Paranormal Research and Defense. Together they take on Nimue (Milla Jovovich), also known as the Blood Queen, who seeks nothing less than the destruction of all mankind. Following the success of Hellboy (2004) and its sequel Hellboy II: The Golden Army, writer/director Guillermo del Toro enthusiastically pursued plans for a third film to complete his cinematic trilogy. When these fell through, Millennium Films and Dark Horse Entertainment developed a reboot with Lloyd Levin, Larry Gordon and Mike Richardson producing. Neil Marshall, who first hit the spotlight with his low budget horror films Dog Soldiers and The Descent, seized the directorial reins. Principal photography for Hellboy took place from October to December 2017, on soundstages at Nu Boyana Film Studios in Bulgaria, and at various locations throughout the United Kingdom. A lengthy postproduction phase followed, lasting almost until the film's release in April 2019. Throughout, the intention was to embrace the violence of the comic books and deliver the first Hellboy film to merit an R rating. Special character designer Joel Harlow and his team of artists at Morphology FX designed all the creatures seen in Hellboy, many of which were ultimately realized by visual effects in digital form. "Daniel Carrasco Jabalera was my primary designer," said Harlow. Richard Luong and Allen Williams were in there too. Most of the time we delivered a finished Z-Brush model; Dave Grasso would render that and we would pass it off to the various effects houses to translate." Harlow broke down the film's monster parade into three distinct categories. iFirst there are all the creatures that live in our world and therefore feel that they belong there. Hellboy himself is a part of that, even though he's actually 2 / 30 from Hell." The second category - dubbed the 'ancient world' - contained creatures

from folklore such as goblins and giants, fairies and sprites. Last but not least came a host of nightmarish demons that rise from the underworld during the film's final act. A third movie outing, Joel Harlow created a makeup for David Harbour that harked back to the earliest Mike Mignola comic artwork from 1993. There is a huge fan base for the other cinematic versions of this character, and we wanted to stay away from that, Harlow stated. 'So I started with the source material - with Mike's illustrations and those of some of the other artists that have lent their skills to translating Hellboy two-dimensionally, like Richard Corben, who is one of my favorite artists, and shaped so much of my childhood. The script described a character who has been around the block a few times, so Harlow made sure to inflict plenty of wear and tear.iThere was a conscious effort to give him skin imperfections and body hair, to make him live and breathe in the world that we all inhabit." Sculptor Joey Orosco translated Hellboy concept art into a clay maquette. With David Harbour already lined up to play the role, Orosco subtly incorporated the actor's features into his sculpture. Harbour underwent a lifecasting session, providing the Morphology FX team with a full-size head and body cast over which to create the final sculpture. Orosco completed the face and head, Mario Torres fashioned the body, and Chris Hamburger tackled the massive Hand of Doom - the sledgehammer appendage that Hellboy HELLBOY Il things began with the story's central character. Rick Baker's Cinovation Studios had created the Hellboy makeup worn by Ron Perlman in the 2004 feature; Spectral Motion revisited the design for the sequel. For the character's 3 / 30

HELLBOY carries at the end of his right arm. After molding, special effects technician Roland Blancaflor ran the body in foam rubber, yielding a one-piece suit with a zipper up the back, cunningly concealed beneath a mane of hair. The suit's left arm ended at the wrist, where it blended into David Harbour's real hand. The right arm plunged straight into the upper section of the Hand of Doom, which comprised a gauntlet section cast in TC-9462 - an exceptionally durable, ultralightweight 60 Shore polyurethane elastomer manufactured by BJB Enterprises - with foam pieces for the palm and fingers. Josh McCarron ran silicone appliances for Hellboy's face and head, including a skullcap with magnetic attachment points for various sets of horns, and separate appliances for the face, lips, ears and back of the head. Contact lenses, dentures and a straggling wig made up the ensemble. Hellboy's tail came in several guises, including a static version and a kinetic variant that swayed naturally as Harbour moved around. Attached to a plate on the actor's belt, the kinetic tail was made from a simple spring steel wire clad in a foam latex sleeve. A more complex cable-controlled tail delivered directable performances to camera. For a scene in which Hellboy's bare feet are visible, David Harbour donned a pair of slipperlike silicone appliances. At a critical point in the story, Hellboy becomes the prophesied Beast of the Apocalypse, at which point his horns grow to a prodigious length. Harbour wore full horns and a 'stage two' set of revved-up prosthetics that exaggerated Hellboy's demonic features, sculpted by Norman Cabrera. "A story point is that his horns are growing all the 4 / 30 time," observed Harlow. "Normally he files them down, so they're continually in a state

of change. That was one of the things that I wanted to do to make him feel more real - keep swapping out the horns to different lengths and surface textures. All the horns made for the film, long and short, were cast in the same plastic material as the Hand of Doom gauntlet. E operation took around two and a half hours - a relatively quick turnaround given that Harbour was almost completely encased from the waist up. It took about an hour to strip everything off again - silicone appliances were discarded while the foam body suit was refurbished for the following day. "We got maybe a week and a half out of the bodies," Harlow reported. "The issue was that he is bare-chested the entire film, and he does a lot more physical fighting than he has before - I mean, he fights everything in this movie! That body suit was getting beat up very regularly and extremely on almost a daily basis so there was a lot of scrambling to do maintenance.i Harlow's team went through a number of iterations before finally hitting just the right balance of vibrancy and realism. The red that you've seen in the prior films is an extreme red," said Harlow. "But when a color is that bright, you can't really paint in skin detail - all you can do is add shadow. I wanted to pull back the red so that I could paint in imperfections, which maintain the believability. HELLBOY little more pale; that allowed us to push areas darker, but also pull areas back where we needed to.i Morphology FX created special effects makeup for other characters including plague victims and a coven of witches. Makeup designer Yana Stoyanova used Prosaid transfers to apply facial scars to Daniel Dae Kim as Ben Daimio. Production designer Paul Kirby steered the overall look of the film, and supervised an extensive set build at Nu Boyana Film Studios. "My background is quite a broad church," commented Kirby. "On one side I've done ultrarealism with films like Captain Phillips, then there's Kingsman: The Secret Service where the design is front-and-center. For Hellboy, I went somewhere between the two.i Kirby found inspiration in the sophisticated color palette from the Hellboy comics.iIf you study the artwork, a lot of beautiful color language emerges. When Hellboy's in the frame, he's the only thing that's red - everything else is much cooler in blues and greens. But if there's something hellish going on, then the whole frame is red and yellow and Hellboy is in a different color. If Hellboy is holding something important - like a sword - it's often golden yellow. The colors themselves are what you might call tertiary colors - slightly off-kilter reds, purples, turquoises. On top of that there are these very deep blacks." Kirby often planned the colors of a set to reflect these themes, such as in a snooker room at the Osiris Club, a secret society obsessed with the occult. "Because Hellboy is the only red thing in the frame as he walks through, I changed all the red snooker balls to black and made just the black ball red. Instead of green, I made the color of the baize on the table turquoise." During preproduction on Hellboy, the art department of Worldwide FX, based in 6 / 30 Sofia, Bulgaria, worked with Neil Marshall and Lloyd Levin to storyboard the entire film,

and created additional concept art for environments and creatures under the direction HELLBOY of Paul Kirby and Joel Harlow. Worldwide FX visual effects supervisor Vesselina Georgieva was present on set throughout the shoot; the company also provided a team of data wranglers to capture camera data, and to scan actors, sets and over 200 props.We ended up shooting in 52 different locations," said Georgieva. "We did photo surveys, photogrammetry and lidar at the locations. We also built a 3D scan stage especially for the film, where we did facial and body scans for all the main actors, plus about 30 extras for crowd replications. We ended up with 12 terabytes of data and more than half a million pictures, which we prepped for all the vendorsi Visual effects producer Danail 'Dundee' Hadzhiyski led proceedings through postproduction until August 2018, when Anna James took up the baton; Hadzhiyski returned later to take the film across the finish line. Worldwide FX handled just over half the film's 1,600-plus visual effects shots. Other vendors included Rhythm & Hues Studios, Mr. X, RISE and Goodbye Kansas, with additional work done by Nvizible and Nu Boyana FX. ¿We broke down the work by sequences and by characters, and created packages based on that," said Hadzhiyski. "If a character was only present in one sequence, that was a package. If they carried on through multiple sequences, that was a separate thing. But overlaps were unavoidable, so sometimes we had the environments in a sequence being done by one vendor and the characters by anotheri Neil Marshall delivered his director's cut in March 2018, at which point postproduction began in earnest with the hiring of overall visual effects supervisor Steve Begg. iMy in7 / 30 volvement on the film was purely accidental," Begg said. "I was in the middle of Soho in

London and I bumped into Lloyd Levin - literally bumped into him; I'd last worked for Lloyd on Lara Croft Tomb Raider: The Cradle of Life. He asked what I was up to, and I told him I was waiting on some projects. 'No,' he said, 'what are you up to right now? At Levin's invitation, Begg began work immediately, anticipating a short-term assignment but ultimately remaining as visual effects supervisor all the way through to final delivery early in 2019. "I was really taken with the project, so I went through a catch-up period and just kind of stuck with it. It was unusual because the visual effects were largely unawarded until well into post." renowned in English folklore as a meeting place for witches. Paul Kirby designed a hilltop set surrounded by bluescreen. "There was just so much action there," Kirby commented. iWe had many different weather patterns, storms and rain, creatures coming out of the ground. We decided to build the top of the hill in the studio so it was more controllable." The set included a cluster of standing stones - an iconic landmark to help audiences identify Pendle Hill in later scenes set in the present day. "We were going to use a village location, but then Neil and Lloyd had this great idea to put these stones in the middle of a supermarket parking lot. When you've got things that are so fantastical, it's nice to subvert that with something ordinary." They originally chose English locations they liked," said Vesselina Georgieva. "But it evolved so much that at the end it was totally new - you will not find this place anywhere in England! Because a lot of magic happens there, we had to add wind effects - all our CG greenery was moving in most of the shots." Nimue's magical powers give her control over nature. Worldwide FX employed Side Effects Houdini simulations to whip up a portal of spinning leaves and debris through which the sorceress teleports from one place to another. Artists also simulated swarms of bugs, used by Nimue to spread a flesh-eating plague. Nimue's magic makes her immortal so, unable to kill her, King Arthur and Merlin instead chop her into six pieces, locking the body parts in separate boxes to be dispatched to the far corners of the world. Worldwide FX splashed blood across the gory dissection scene and crafted a fullyCG closeup of the moment when Nimue is decapitated. "It was something we'd never done before - a digi-double of a main actor in closeup," Georgieva remarked. "It was a technical challenge for our studio because everyone knows what Milla Jovovich looks like." The team used Autodesk Reality Capture photogrammetry software to record the actress pulling over 60 different facial expressions, then refined the resulting geometry in Pixologic Z-Brush and Autodesk Maya. "We did a full simulation of her beautiful long hair, and put in a lot of blood!i Worldwide FX animators applied motion capture performances to six CG 'creatures of darkness' seen during the Pendle Hill prologue. 9 / 30 At the suggestion of Steve Begg, the prologue underwent radical desaturation in the

digital intermediate. "I came up with the idea sitting in a pub," Begg recalled. "I had my laptop with me, with Adobe Photoshop on it, and I was looking at images from this opening sequence. While they looked good, in color they had a hell of a theatrical look about them. So I started fooling about with desaturating them, doing a color bias. Finally I just turned them all into black and white and, whoa, I got this fantastic 1930s Universal horror film look. Now it looked intentionally theatrical. The sweetener on top was that Nimue dresses in red, so in the DI we isolated her so she's the only red thing in the shot. The red theme really kick-starts the movie, and then carries all the way throughi ings with Rhythm & Hues, which populated the enchanted hilltop with swarms of fairies, goblins and sprites, and delivered the shots back as final composites. Tasked with enhancing the facial performance, Rhythm & Hues built a CG Gruagach comprising the character's head and upper body, based on scans and photogrammetry of the practical creature. "Initially we thought about using Ptex remapping," said Rhythm & Hues visual effects supervisor John Haley. Rhythm & Hues has a history with this technique for talking creatures going back to Babe, and a pipeline that's very robust. Worldwide FX did environment duties again, but this time shared assets and background paintOne of Nimue's loyal acolytes is the boar-man Gruagach. On set, performer Douglas 10 / 30

HELLBOY getting enough articulation in the boar's snout and around the eyes. We found that we had a better result out of the gate with a full CG head replacement. Artists at Rhythm & Hues rotomated the live-action, locking the CG head and torso to Tait's movements. Animation supervisor James Kinnings and his team then brought Gruagach fully to life. "Midway through production, our rigging supervisor, Matt Derkson, set up this amazing tool where you could use video tootage to drive the Gruagach puppet," Haley revealed. "Oftentimes, the animators would film themselves speaking the lines and use this facial animation tool to do an initial blocking pass. Then they would go in and do the rest with keyframes. We settled on a performance that was as realistic as possible given the nature of the character - not too hammy and over-emoted. Artists positioned the split line at different points along Gruagach's torso, typically just below the pectoral muscles. Rhythm & Hues CG supervisor Dante Quintana and his look development team matched the coarse-furred appearance of the practical Gruagach.iWe applied the textures to the animation puppet, so we had this beefy upper torso and head that was fully textured and lit, sitting within the playblast that the animators would output. Right out of the gate, Steve Begg would get a good indication of what the entire shot was going to look like." Rhythm & Hues created a fully CG baby Gruagach for a flashback sequence that reveals the character's origins as a fairy changeling swapped at birth with the infant Alice Monaghan. Rhythm & Hues transformed a CG baby Alice limb by limb into the foulmouthed boar-child. Channeling the irascible Baby Herman from Who Framed Roger I1 / 30 Rabbit?, animators took the character's gruff dialogue and ran with it - literally, for a

HELLBOY scene in which baby Gruagach tries to escape the clutches of Hellboy, who is present at the scene. "There was a lot of great on-set interaction driven by the special effects guys," noted Haley. "We painted out the rigs, and the animation team did an amazing job of blocking the shots to choreograph Gru's actions with all the wire pulls." Hellboy snags baby Gruagach with a set of fire tongs, which burn his iron-phobic flesh. Artists at Rhythm & Hues added digital smoke to shots of the tongs searing the changeling's skin. Rhythm & Hues expanded its child-sized portfolio by creating a fully CG infant Hellboy for a separate flashback sequence. Following the prologue on Pendle Hill, the story leaps to modern-day Tijuana, Mexico, where Hellboy has tracked missing BPRD operative Camazotz (Mario de la Rosa) to a lucha libre wrestling bout. When Camazotz transforms unexpectedly into a were-bat, Hellboy takes to the ring to engage him in fisticuffs. Production shot the fight twice, once with David Harbour grappling Mario de la Rosa, and a second time with stunt doubles dialing up the action. Artists at the London office of Worldwide FX painted out the live-action Camazotz and replaced him with a CG creature designed by Morphology FX, meticulously tracked to maintain contact with Hellboy during the close-quarters fight. Animators also handled complex transformation shots, including the climactic moment when, impaled on a ringside stanchion, Camazotz finally reverts to human form. Back at the BPRD base in Colorado, Hellboy picks up an assignment that takes him to England - specifically the headquarters of the Osiris Club. Worldwide FX created establishing shots for both locations. For a wide shot of the BPRD base, artists rendered a 12 / 30 digital matte painting of the sleek building nestled amid mountain scenery, while ani-

mators piloted a CG helicopter through flurries of simulated snow. Production photographed Osiris Club exteriors at Grittleton House near Bristol in the UK; Worldwide FX enhanced establishing shots of the Victorian manor house with CG vehicles. D "The corridor felt a little comic to me — it didn't have any jeopardy," remarked Paul Kirby. I designed this octagonal space with about a dozen giants' heads of varying history and decay glaring down on you from above. That way the camera could spin around Hellboy and the other characters and give it an unnerving feeling. Constructed from plaster and latex, the heads ranged from four to six times human size. The art and props departments filled the surrounding cabinets with the remains of weird creatures, including a desiccated mermaid and a skeleton with a human head perched on spider's legs. Hellboy joins members of the Osiris Club on a ritual giant-hunting expedition, but in the wilds of England the huntsmen turn traitor and try to kill him. Hellboy survives only to find himself fighting for his life against the very giants they were looking for in the first place. Artists at Nvizible energized the huntsmen's weapons with electrocution effects. Nvizible also delivered shots for another fight in which various witch characters are shot and killed, using particle effects to simulate souls being punched out of the bodies of the slaughtered hags. Production shot the prelude and aftermath of Hellboy's battle with the giants on locaHELLBOY eep inside the Osiris Club, Hellboy enters a room filled with occult artifacts, including the mounted heads of slain giants. Production staged the action on an imposing set that strayed from the trophy-lined corridor described in the script. 13 / 30

HELLBOY tion in the United Kingdom, but staged the main action on a stage at Nu Boyana. There, David Harbour and stuntmen performed on a small patch of grassland surrounded by bluescreen, with blue bucks and set pieces representing various parts of the giants' anatomy. Initially reliant on multiple cuts, the fight developed during postproduction into a bravura battle built around a single long take; this was eventually split into two segments, the first lasting 2,300 frames and the second 2,500 frames. Mr. X - which handled visual effects for the entire giant fight - built up the sequence in postvis like a jigsaw puzzle, stitching together multiple live-action plates, plotting camera moves devised by the production editorial team, and executing bits of animated action to creatively join the dots. Elaborating on Joel Harlow's concept designs, Mr. X visual effects supervisor Chris McLean oversaw the asset team creating Hellboy's three jumbo-sized adversaries, each named after the weapon he favors. With just one eye, the Axe Giant became known as 'Cyclops,' while the Sword Giant earned the nickname 'Slash'; the Club Giant was simply 'Clubber.' "The models were very complex," said Mr. X visual effects supervisor James Cooper. "Our creature development team worked non-stop on muscle simulation, skin, fat and facial rigs, and all the subsurface scattering in the skin. The giants wear pelts of skin and jangly armor cobbled together from tires and car doors, and one has a human torso on his belly, so there were a lot of complicated simulationsi Motion capture sessions kicked off the giants' performances, subsequently refined by animators at Mr. X. "We had to mess with the scale," commented Mr. X animation director Kevin Scott. ¿The giants are anywhere from 23 to 26 feet tall, so we did physically 14 / 30 accurate gravity tests to determine the realistic rate of movement for creatures this big.

HELLBOY We ended up making the stunt guys do all the actions twice as fast and then we slowed them down by half." Performers sometimes strapped weights to their arms to increase the sense of mass. Those playing Slash, who has a lame leg and arm, wore inserts in their shoes to keep them off-balance. The hard part was having them not act like giants - the stunt guys always wanted to do everything in slow motion. We would keep telling them, 'Just go and beat the crap out of each other, and we'll take care of the rest."" Mr. X fashioned the broad expanse of open countryside across which Hellboy and the giants pursue their tussle.iAt one point Hellboy grabs the stump of a tree and uses it as a javelin to hit Slash in the face," James Cooper explained. "It didn't make sense to have this one stump in the middle of an otherwise empty meadow, so we added in various copses. Mr. X also replicated real-world settings from the shoot location, such as the river where the huntsmen leave Hellboy for dead, and the forest beyond it. Artists grew trees and vegetation using IDV SpeedTree, and surrounded the CG landscape with digital matte paintings of mountains and a sky dome. Effects artists simulated ground disturbances and sprays of dirt kicked up by the combatants as they trade blows. For certain beats - such as when Clubber knocks Hellboy more or less out of the park - Mr. X brought out a Hellboy digi-double. With the action snapping between the live-action Hellboy and his CG counterpart throughout the long takes, the segues between real and digital realms had to be seamless.iOur comp leads Alessandro Pantanella and Jeremy Johnson did deep compositing in Nuke to integrate the plate photography into 3D physical space," said Cooper. "One of the toughest bits was when Hellboy runs 15 / 30 and jumps off one of the giant's knees. He lands on the giant's head and shoulders and

begins to pummel him. They had got the stunt double to jump up onto a big blue mechanical rig, but unfortunately his legs kept disappearing behind the blue areas. At one point we considered turning that whole segment into a Hellboy digi-double, but with some creative jogging we managed to pull it together." Gargantuan gouts of blood provided the final garnish as each giant meets his gory demise. Seeking spectacular reference for the bloodletting, Lloyd Levin and Steve Begg steered their visual effects vendors towards the Starz television series American Gods. "Unbeknownst to them, I was visual effects supervisor on that show here at Mr. X," Cooper said. 'There's a big Viking battle in season one, and we had done all the blood work on that - torrential rains of blood flying everywhere. We went that extreme for this fight, especially when the final giant loses an arm and a leg before getting his skull split open by Hellboy." through a combination of prosthetic makeup by Joel Harlow and visual effects by Rhythm & Hues. "Baba Yaga is definitely the stuff of nightmares," said John Haley. "I had the unfortunate experience of reading some of the Russian fairy tales about her when I was a kid. She's generally depicted as wearing a necklace of children's ears or skulls or other body parts. I used to have nightmares about her sneaking into my room and chopping off my feet!" HELLBOY lants are by no means the strangest creatures that Hellboy encounters on his travels. Zapped between dimensions, he also pays a visit to Baba Yaga, a child-eating witch notorious in Russian folklore and brought to the screen 16 / 30

HELLBOY Hellboy discovers Baba Yaga in a misty forest, where her wooden house roams around on giant chicken legs. Production shot exterior scenes on a blank white set, leaving Rhythm & Hues to embed the live-action into a CG forest and create the witch's weird ambulatory home. Paul Kirby designed Baba Yaga's house, inspired partly by the Sutyagin House, a towering residence constructed by mobster Nikolai Petrovich Sutyagin in the Russian coastal city of Arkhangelsk. At 144 feet high, the building was once thought to be the tallest wooden house in the world, but was condemned before completion and has since been demolished. Artists at Rhythm & Hues built up the house digitally. "We referenced a bunch of Russian churches with nice spire pieces and wooden shingle details," Haley said, "as well as wooden Siberian houses with this driftwood feel - generally, they don't paint them, because it's so cold that the paint doesn't adhere to the wood. Rhythm & Hues grafted the finished house onto a pair of legs based on those of the Russian Orloff breed of chicken. Stomping up to meet Hellboy, the house squats and allows him to enter. The production art department designed a minimal exterior set - just one doorway and a section of window. Rhythm & Hues extended or replaced the live-action. "Often, we would just postage-stamp the plate onto our CG Baba Yaga house," related Haley. "Once we had the plate projected in there, we would generally override the camera move from set with a CG move that our animation team would set up, because our CG house was ten times larger than what was shot." 17 / 30 The house is much bigger on the inside than it appears from the outside. The interior

HELLBOY set included a larder stocked with a stomach-churning smörgåsbord of children's giblets, simulated with cold cuts, pork ribs and prop skulls. Rhythm & Hues extended Paul Kirby's macabre set into an infinite hallway. Once inside the house, Hellboy comes face to face with Baba Yaga, played by contortionist and America's Got Talent contestant Troy James, popularly known as 'Twisty Troy.' The Power Within Her BY JOE FORDHAM arvel movie audiences have learned to wait, as end credits roll, for extra scenes tagged onto the latest superhero epic. Perhaps one of the most enigmatic post-credit teasers occurred after Avengers: Infinity War when - spoiler alert - most of the cast crumbled into dust, and S.H.I.E.L.D. colonel Nick Fury (Samuel Jackson) sent a message to an operative identified only by an eight-pointed star with a red and blue background. Fans quickly deciphered the cryptic coda based on a revelation, at the 2016 San Diego Comic-Con, announcing Brie Larson as the star of the upcoming Captain Marvel. Casting of the Oscar-winning performer in the role of Carol Danvers - former United States Air Force pilot turned intergalactic superhero - marked a milestone in the series, introducing one of comic book lore's most powerful heroes. Yet, this was not a typical origin story. "The story was not simply about Carol being given her powers," observed visual effects supervisor Christopher Townsend.iThe idea was that Carol uses powers within her as her strength. It was an empowerment story, with a strong female lead who uses her innate abilities to create this incredible superheroi 1 / 38 Townsend spearheaded a roster of visual effects produced by teams in 10 cities on

three continents. "We like to diversify," noted visual effects producer Damien Carr. "And CAPTAIN MARVEL we like to keep each studio to under 400 shots because they need to be able to move, and move quickly. If artists become bogged down with more than 400 shots, it becomes much more difficult for them to handle changes.i The production ended up working with 14 visual effects studios: ILM, Trixter, Digital Domain, Lola VFX, Screen Scene VFX, Rising Sun Pictures, Scanline VFX, Framestore, Luma Pictures, RISE Visual Effects Studios, Animal Logic and DNEG. Cantina Creative provided motion graphic design, and Exceptional Minds handled rotoscoping and composites. Marvel stereographic supervisor Evan Jacobs oversaw stereographic conversions. Christopher Townsend, executive producer Jonathan Shwartz and Damien Carr joined the production after completing Marvel Studios' Guardians of the Galaxy Vol. 2, and met with directors Anna Boden and Ryan Fleck - co-creators of the indie dramas Half Nelson and Mississippi Grind - to discuss their take on the character. The screenplay - by Boden, Fleck and Geneva Robertson-Dworet - introduced Carol Danvers as 'Vers,' human member of the intergalactic Starforce peacekeeping team on the Kree homeworld of Hala. There, Carol is haunted by hazy recollections of life on Earth, which resurface when Kree commander Yon-Rogg (Jude Law) dispatches her on a mission, and shapeshifter Skrulls attempt to probe Carol's memories. Carol escapes to Earth, 1995, and falls in with a young government agent, Nick Fury, who helps her confront a mystery surrounding Skrull invader, Talos (Ben Mendelsohn), which causes Carol to reconcile her destiny as a hybrid human-superhero, Captain Marvel. 2 / 38 The plot incorporated aspects of comic book creators Stan Lee and Gene Colan's

original concepts with the character's later incarnations. "We were moved by the character that Kelly Sue Deconnick had written for Carol Danvers in the series," said Anna Boden. Her flaws, her messiness, and her humanity made her fascinating. That was the character we discussed in our talks with Brie. We were after somebody who, at the beginning of the movie, doesn't know herself entirely. Later, she discovers what she needs to become her most powerful self.i W and Ryan came from a practical film background and their first instincts were to shoot as much as possible for real. The challenge for us was to keep the action as grounded as possible, but also to create new worlds, which were different and alien, but not as fantastical as those in Guardians. The Elephant in the Room BY JODY DUNCAN hen the Walt Disney Company's third animated feature film - the ambitious Fantasia, released in 1940 - failed to score at the box office, Disney sought to recoup his losses the following year with a shorter and more modest fourth offering, Dumbo. Based on a children's story by Helen Aberson, Dumbo's simple narrative followed the exploits of a baby elephant with ears so enormous he becomes the laughingstock of the circus into which he is born - that is, until those same ears enable him to fly, turning Dumbo into a Big Top headliner. nearly 80 years later, Walt Disney Pictures presents a live-action feature film version of the story, directed by Tim Burton and starring Colin Farrell, Eva Green, Michael Keaton and Danny DeVito. Given that Dumbo and the film's other circus animals would be computer animated characters delivered by MPC, under the direction of production visual effects supervisor Richard Stammers and visual effects producer Hal Couzens, previs executed by The Third Floor was an integral part of the project's development as Burton and his crews prepared 1/31 for principal photography at Pinewood Studios.i On a show where your main character

is digital," noted Hal Couzens, "you rely on previs more than you might otherwise. The Nature of the Beast BY GRAHAM EDWARDS ince the earliest days of cinema, filmmakers have delighted in putting animals in front of the camera, and audiences have thrilled to their exploits. In 1922, a German Shepherd named Rin Tin Tin played the part of a wolf in the western The Man from Hell's River and secured his place as the world's first canine movie star. After a 1938 film debut in The Adventures of Robin Hood, a palomino called Golden Cloud acquired the name Trigger and became almost as famous as Roy Rogers, the cowboy actor who rode him throughout countless subsequent movies. In 1943, audiences sobbed when Lassie came home. Life has not always been easy for Hollywood's animal performers. The early dominance of the western and the historical epic encouraged stunt coordinators to devise ever more cunning ways to show animals in jeopardy - and sometimes to put their lives at risk. One notorious trick was the 'running W,' which caused a horse to fall to the ground at a predetermined spot. First, wires were attached to cuffs on the horse's forelegs. These wires ran up through metal rings beneath the saddle cinches, then extended back to a 1 / 36 stake bedded into the ground at a set distance behind. The horse was spurred to a gallop

DIGITAL ANIMALS and at the designated moment the wires tightened, pulling the legs up and back and causing the unfortunate animal to crash earthwards. More often than not, the injuries sustained in the stunt meant the horse had to be destroyed. As awareness grew about such cavalier attitudes toward animal safety, so too did the influence of various animal welfare organizations. In 1941, following publicity over disputed animal cruelty during the making of the 1939 film Jesse James, the society known as American Humane for the first time published a set of formal standards covering the treatment of animals in film production, and the Association of Motion Picture Producers agreed henceforth to open movie sets to its representatives. Since then, attitudes involving animal safety and welfare have continued to mature, and American Humane's trademarked 'No Animals Were Harmed' certification in end credits - issued for the first time to the bank heist caper The Doberman Gang in 1972 - is now sought by most self-respecting film producers as a matter of course. But what are these same producers to do when their stories demand animal action that lies outside the safety standards? If lost pets do not face mortal danger, why should audiences care whether or not they make it home? In every stampede, horses must fall. Luckily for filmmakers, bloodless substitutes for real animals have always been available, from animated models to animatronic puppets and beyond. For Mighty Joe Young in 1949, Willis O Brien and Ray Harryhausen wrangled stop-motion lions in a nightclub rampage scene - and of course brought the film's titular 10-foot-tall gorilla to life. Decades later, Rick Baker dressed a troupe of suit performers in exquisite ape costumes for the 2 / 36 1984 feature Greystoke: The Legend of Tarzan, Lord of the Apes.

Since the closing years of the 20th century, however, a wholly different kind of animal has evolved, one whose performance is limited neither by physical constraints nor welfare organization guidelines - and these cutting-edge creatures are not your typical cats and dogs. Where nature builds its lifeforms by assembling proteins, lipids and polysaccharides around a DNA blueprint, the newcomers are constructed from pixels. Four and a half billion years after it first formed, planet Earth is now home to the digital beast. instead. But the action does not need to be so extreme. A regular film set crowded with crew, glaring with lights and crisscrossed with cables is a stressful place for any animal to be, by default. Next, consider the many occasions when the script calls for animals to do impossible things. When the horse must leap the uncrossable canyon, or the pig must converse with her farmyard friends, these are the times when cinematic illusions must be deployed.
